rows: Sex used to release frustration, anxiety, or stress. Higher scores may indicate that sex serves an emotion-regulation function.
Sex motivated by physical enjoyment and desire. Typically among the most frequently endorsed motivations.
Sex motivated by attraction to the other person’s appearance. The items refer to the person rather than a partner, reflecting that the measure covers casual and non-partnered sex.
Sex pursued for novelty, adventure, or excitement.
Sex exchanged for tangible gain such as money or favours. Elevated scores indicate that exchange-based motivations feature in the respondent’s experiences.
Sex motivated by the desire to conceive. Scores are strongly context-dependent and interpreted in light of life stage and relationship circumstances.
Sex used to enhance reputation or standing.
Sex used to retaliate against a partner or get even with someone. Elevated scores may indicate unresolved relational conflict.
Sex pursued for practical benefits. The two items span distinct content, one physical and one emotional, so reviewing them individually shows which is driving the score.
Sex used to express love and feel connected. Low scores in a partnered respondent may be clinically informative about the relational function of sex.
Sex used to mark special occasions or transitions, such as welcomes, farewells, and celebrations.
Sex used to feel better about oneself. Elevated scores may indicate that sexual activity is serving a self-worth regulation function.
Sex engaged in out of obligation or in response to pressure. Elevated scores can reflect experiences of sexual coercion.
Sex used to keep a partner from straying. Elevated scores may indicate relationship insecurity or fear of abandonment.
